correctness.rationale: Proof checks exact graph edges, every subset of sizes 1–7, all legal one-edge collision-free simultaneous moves by a perfect-matching equivalence, and full fatal-attack complements for all 790 dominating states of sizes six and seven. Direct Python move enumeration and a distinct C++ pairwise matching enumeration agree on 10 six-guard states (two fatal attacks each), 780 seven-guard states, the 20 unique \(S_1(x)\cup S_4(x)\cup S_5(x)\) traps, 760 closed winning states and exact minimum 26 safe responses. The finite certificate records 9,880 winning attack responses, each checked by an additional subset-matching program. The proof of infinite defense is induction on attacks over a finite attack-closed set; no finite experiment alone substitutes for that induction.

originality.rationale: Full-text comparisons against the 2014 general model paper and 2021 \(\operatorname{GP}(n,2)\) strategy paper show that the seven-guard existence construction and six-vertex ordinary domination are prior knowledge, but do not give a count or geometric description of all winning and losing seven-guard placements. The present 760/20 state-space classification, all immediate fatal attacks, and sharp minimum of 26 safe one-step responses were not covered by inspected sources. Nine topic-specific mathematical-record queries and targeted scholarly searches supplied no stronger covering theorem; novelty remains conditional on accessible literature.
residual_risks: Equivalent results may exist in unindexed publications, repositories, conference supplements or alternative guard-game terminology.

value.rationale: The gap between existence of a seven-guard perpetual defense and a complete classification of which placements can actually defend is a natural strategy-synthesis problem. The twenty exceptions have a canonical intrinsic description by three distance spheres, while all other seven-guard dominating sets form an attack-closed safety kernel, with a sharp positive minimum of 26 distinct replies. This establishes structural geometry and tactical redundancy in a canonical cubic graph, independent of generalization to infinitely many graphs.
